flashcards.q: What is the four-era lineage of search ranking, and what specific failure motivated each transition?
flashcards.a: Boolean (no ranking, match/no-match) -> TF-IDF/BM25 (fixes ranking, but vocabulary mismatch: "car" never matches "automobile") -> dense bi-encoder (fixes vocabulary mismatch, but blurs rare/exact tokens like SKUs) -> hybrid (fuses both, complementary failure modes) -> learned ranking (adds business signals no text-similarity method can see).

flashcards.q: What are typical recall@10 numbers comparing hybrid, dense-only, and sparse-only retrieval?
flashcards.a: Roughly 91% recall@10 for hybrid vs. 78% dense-only vs. 65% sparse-only in typical production benchmarks.

flashcards.q: Name three concrete cases where BM25 still beats embeddings, and the mechanism in each.
flashcards.a: (1) Exact identifiers (SKUs, error codes) -- rare tokens an embedding model never anchored well; BM25's IDF finds the literal string. (2) Rare technical/domain jargon, same reason. (3) Code search -- identifiers are precise structured tokens; users want exact symbol matches, not "semantically similar" code.

flashcards.q: How does learned-to-rank (LTR) differ from a cross-encoder reranker?
flashcards.a: A cross-encoder reranker scores query-document text relevance only. LTR takes a feature vector per query-candidate pair (which can include the cross-encoder's score as one input) plus business signals -- CTR, recency, price, personalization, inventory -- that no text-similarity model can see, and trains a model to optimize a ranking metric like nDCG over the combined set.

flashcards.q: What is LambdaMART and why has it remained a production standard?
flashcards.a: A gradient-boosted decision tree ranker (building on RankNet/LambdaRank, formalized ~2010) trained to directly optimize a ranking metric like nDCG rather than pointwise regression. Won the 2010 Yahoo! LTR Challenge; remains standard because GBDTs handle nonlinear feature interactions well, train fast, and are cheap/predictable to serve versus a neural ranker.

flashcards.q: Describe the four-stage cascade architecture used in large-scale search/ads ranking.
flashcards.a: Matching (cheap, corpus-scale candidate generation via inverted index/ANN) -> pre-ranking (lightweight model narrows millions to thousands) -> ranking (full LTR/neural model scores thousands down to tens) -> mix-ranking (business rules: diversity, ad interleaving, dedup) before serving.

flashcards.q: What is position bias in LTR training data, and how do you correct for it?
flashcards.a: Users click higher-ranked results more often regardless of true relevance because they rarely scroll to fairly evaluate lower results. Training on raw click logs teaches the model to reinforce the existing ranking, not true relevance. Fix: inverse propensity scoring (weight clicks by inverse probability of being seen at that position) or randomized result interleaving.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom that an LTR model is suffering from position bias?
flashcards.a: Offline ranking metrics (e.g. nDCG on click-derived labels) improve steadily while online engagement metrics stay flat or regress -- that divergence is the signature symptom.

flashcards.q: Why can query rewriting (HyDE, keyword expansion) hurt retrieval instead of helping it?
flashcards.a: It can distort the original query's intent or overamplify rare terms the user never cared about, shifting retrieval toward a subtly different question. This is a documented failure mode, not hypothetical -- it needs per-query-type eval, not blanket application.

flashcards.q: When is a full LTR layer the wrong investment?
flashcards.a: When there isn't enough real interaction/click data -- small catalogs, low traffic, cold-start. A GBDT trained on sparse/synthetic labels overfits noise; hand-tuned boosting (weighted BM25 + recency + popularity, e.g. Elasticsearch function scoring) is more transparent and just as effective at that scale.

flashcards.q: What is the honest default answer to "which retrieval architecture should we ship first"?
flashcards.a: Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense, RRF-fused) plus a cross-encoder reranker over the fused shortlist, validated against a recall@k/nDCG eval. A full learned-ranking layer with business features is additional investment justified only when there's a business objective beyond relevance AND enough interaction data to train on.

flashcards.q: Why can't reranking or LTR fully compensate for weak retrieval or reranking below them?
flashcards.a: Each layer in the stack can only reorder what the layer below already surfaced. A business-aware LTR model cannot promote a genuinely relevant item that hybrid retrieval never put in the candidate set to begin with.

flashcards.q: In marketplace search with sponsored listings, should sponsored placement be blended into the LTR score or kept separate?
flashcards.a: Keep sponsored listings as a distinct mix-ranking step interleaved after organic ranking, not blended into the same LTR score, so ranking transparency and auditability (e.g. proving sponsored placement doesn't bias organic relevance) are preserved.
